In Tangent

GeometryCirclesTriangles
What it shows: Two circles sit inside the triangles made by a point X on the bottom side.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or X, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick "Show circle" to see the big circle.
Look for the math

Move X along the bottom side and watch the bright line. Its crossing with the base does not move: it lands on the same dot every time. That is the theorem on the original page, and the logic test checks it on hundreds of triangles rather than just this one.

Two incircles and two tangents

Let IB and IC be the centres of the incircles of triangles ABX and ACX. The line AX touches both circles, so it is one common tangent. Reflect A and X in the line IBIC: each circle is its own mirror image, so the reflected line is the other internal common tangent. The applet draws exactly that line, and the green dot is where it crosses BC.

The crossing is always T

Let T be where the incircle of the whole triangle ABC touches BC. With s = (AB + BC + CA)/2 the semiperimeter, its distance from B is BT = s − CA. The page claims the bright line passes through this fixed point, whatever X does. It also claims TX = TBTC, the gap between the two contact points on AX: if BX = x and XC = y, both sides equal (x − y − AB + CA)/2. The test checks this at every configuration. Equal tangent lengths from S and X then force SB' = XC' and S = T.

The circle through X and T

The dashed circle has diameter IBIC, so its centre is their midpoint and its radius is half their distance. At X the two angle bisectors split angles BXA and CXA, which add to a straight angle; they are perpendicular. The same is true at T for the two tangents. By Thales' theorem, both X and T lie on that circle. The numerical check confirms both distances to its centre equal its radius.

The eyes, and one old quirk

The three little eyes light up only when X is within one unit of T — that is the applet's own Finished test, a hint, not a win. The theorem is true for every other X too; the "Put X at T" button is a modern shortcut to the lit-up picture. The applet's code also holds an unused switch for drawing excircles, but no control reaches it: this port keeps only the incircles, as the page does. The logic test compares the core with a second transcription of the applet's own incenter, reflection and line-intersection methods over hundreds of triangles, and finds |S − T| below the test's 10−4 user-unit tolerance (in practice around 10−12).

Try Put X at T, then tick Show circle: the green circle runs through both the highlighted dot and the X handle.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
